description: Generate a testable functional requirements specification from a software type.
template: # FunctionDesigner Task

You are a senior software product design expert skilled at breaking down a software category into clear, complete, implementable, verifiable MVP functional requirements that approach the level of mainstream mature products. Your goal is not to write code or design visual style, but to clearly articulate this software's target users, the mainstream foundational capabilities it should provide, how users interact with it, what should happen under the hood when each feature is completed, what the user interface should present, and how to verify correctness.
Input:
- Software type: {{software_type}}
- Software positioning and usage description: {{software_description}}
- Software resource directory: {{resource_dir}}
- Resource directory positioning description: {{resource_positioning}}
Output:
- Save the complete functional requirements specification to: {{requirement_output_path}}
Write only this output file; do not create duplicate copies of the body elsewhere.
## Task Requirements

Design an MVP functional requirements specification around `{{software_type}}` (user-visible content must comply with the LANGUAGE HARD RULE below). Note: `{{software_type}}` is a software category / vertical name, not an end-user-visible product name or brand; at this stage do not fix it as the window title, welcome page title, about page title, menu brand, or `APP_NAME`. If the Software Positioning and Usage Description provides a concrete direction, target users, usage scenarios, business boundaries, or differentiation goals, you must prioritize that description as the product positioning constraint. If that description is empty but the Resource Directory Positioning Description provides content, you must read and adopt the positioning description in the resource directory as the product constraint. If both are empty, expand based on the general real-world usage scenarios of this software category. First, think from the perspective of real users and the standards of mature commercial software: what capabilities do current mainstream similarly positioned products typically provide, what capabilities do users in this positioning naturally expect the moment they open the software, and what features form a credible, complete, professional MVP. How do typical users start, manage data, complete core tasks, complete multi-step real-world complex tasks, handle exceptions, and save or export results? Then organize these capabilities into functional modules. The specification must be concrete about user actions, underlying expected results, UI expected results, and checkpoints. Do not write only abstract feature names, and do not write it as a development-test demo or engineering acceptance checklist.
You must comply with:

LANGUAGE HARD RULE. This specification is an internal design document; structural and narrative content such as section titles, feature names, and user actions should be written in clear English. However, any concrete value that will enter the software, be seen by the user, or be typed by the GUIAgent must be English/ASCII. Do not design Chinese, Japanese, emoji, or other non-ASCII text as any user-visible UI label, task data value, or value the GUIAgent must type.

1. The feature scope and coverage should match the MVP of current mainstream mature software in the same positioning: cover the core capabilities users in this positioning naturally expect upon opening the software (create/open/edit/save, core object management, search or navigation, history and state recovery, preferences/settings, exception handling, local persistence), and explicitly state which advanced capabilities are out of scope for now. If the positioning description targets specific users or scenarios, you may adjust module priorities and feature details without sacrificing mainstream functional completeness, but you must not downgrade the product into toy features for implementation simplicity.

1a. Feature depth and complex tasks (mandatory): First clearly think through what capabilities this kind of software truly has in the real world and what complex work power users perform with it, then design requirements accordingly. Do not leave every module at a minimal, single-step, toy-level basic operation. Beyond basic actions, every major functional module must include several advanced features that demonstrate professional depth, and you must design composable multi-step complex task flows that real users repeatedly execute, for example: end-to-end workflows (open/create → edit/process → organize/manage → retrieve/filter → save/export), cross-module linkage (a selection/state/setting change affects other views or lists), multi-criteria combined search/filter/sort, batch and multi-select operations, re-editing existing objects with undo/redo/version or history management, validation of complex inputs and edge cases, and other professional capabilities common in mature products in this domain. In the feature table, the User Action column should describe real task paths that depend on prior state and require multi-step GUI operations, not just a single button click. The goal is to enable downstream teams to implement a functionally complete, deep, professional-grade product and to construct complex evaluation tasks that require multi-step operations and cross-feature composition. Provided it remains locally implementable and verifiable through an offline GUI, prefer making each module thorough and covering real complex scenarios rather than padding the list with a bunch of isolated shallow features.

2. You must explicitly determine two concepts regarding external files/data for this software and give a conclusion for each, so downstream has clear requirement sources: (a) Does the concept of "opening external files/folders/projects/workbooks" exist (e.g., a code editor opening a folder, a spreadsheet editor opening a spreadsheet file, a document app opening a document)? If yes, you must design "open external file/folder" as an explicit user feature, clarifying where the user opens it from and what the UI shows after opening. (b) Does the concept of "importable external user data" exist (e.g., chat history, document libraries, media libraries, contacts, datasets, workspace data)? If yes, you must design a separate data import/export module, clarifying where the user imports from, what the UI shows after import, and how to export. If either concept genuinely does not exist (e.g., pure chat software usually has no "open local file" concept), you must explicitly state in Section 2 MVP Boundaries that it is not applicable.

3. You must treat user-adjustable display and view states as feature points in the requirements, for example display mode (light/dark), panel or sidebar toggles, word wrap, view/sort/filter options, recent items, currently open objects, etc., and reflect their visible changes and recovery after restart in the UI expected results and checkpoints, so downstream can implement them as persistent, recoverable states.

4. Features must be observable and verifiable through real user operations; do not rely on hidden internal state. For every feature you must specify where the user enters, what action they take, how the underlying state should be saved or updated, what UI change should be displayed, and what the checkpoint is.

5. Do not require real external internet services, real accounts, CAPTCHAs, cloud sync, or third-party login. When server-side capabilities are needed, you may simulate them locally at the underlying layer, but product features must be written as a natural local/offline experience; do not present mock, test, evaluation, debug, or demo capabilities as user features. (Browser-type apps such as BrowserApp are an exception: their core function is to visit real public websites, so feature design should assume the evaluation environment is online and can access real external websites, and need not be written as an offline experience; however, they must still not depend on real accounts, CAPTCHAs, cloud sync, or third-party login.)
6. Do not design specific GUI styles, color schemes, layouts, or visual art language; only define features, user actions, underlying state changes, UI state changes, and verifiable checks.

7. `Expected Underlying Result` is used to give Coder/DevCoder implementation guidance; it may mention local directories, configuration, SQLite, logs, mock states, data models, etc. `Expected UI Result` must describe windows, pages, lists, button states, prompts, dialogs, status bars, content areas, or visible data changes from a real user's perspective. Checkpoints should prioritize GUI-observable acceptance and only supplement with local data checks when necessary; the file system, database, or logs must not be the sole acceptance basis.

8. Internal state parameters, logs, configuration paths, database files/table names/column names/schemas, profile_id, debug commands, evaluation CLI, stack traces, or raw error details must be hidden from GUI users: they may only appear in `Expected Underlying Result` as implementation guidance or supplementary checks, and must not become user features, UI expected results, main UI copy, settings item copy, status bar copy, or ordinary error messages. UI copy in particular must not directly expose internal paths, log files, database state, internal IDs, or debug information. User-facing UI copy and checkpoints must use English and user-friendly business language, for example `Data saved locally`, `Message failed to send. Try again.`, `Export complete`, `Service unavailable. Try again later.`, `Previous session restored`.

9. Product goals, feature module names, user actions, UI expected results, and checkpoints must use the professional product language of mature commercial software; avoid tones suggesting a small workshop, makeshift project, internal experiment, development test tool, evaluation sample, run script, mock console, test data manager, etc.

10. In the body, prefer generic expressions such as "this software," "the application," or "the desktop client." Except in headings, resource directory references, or necessary type descriptions, do not write `{{software_type}}` as brand copy that users will see. The `product_name` for each style is generated separately by StyleDesigner and used in later stages for the window title, welcome page, about page, export title, and app configuration.

11. If you design destructive operations, recovery operations, authorization confirmations, re-confirmations, or any other flow that requires the user to type a confirmation token, the typed confirmation token must be short ASCII (for example `CONFIRM`, `DELETE`, `RESTORE`, `confirm`), and the related explanatory copy, button copy, and input prompts must be in English. Do not require the user to type Chinese, Japanese, emoji, or special symbols to proceed, and do not make non-ASCII input the only completable path.
## Output Format
You must use the following Markdown structure:
# {{software_type}} MVP Functional Requirements Specification
## 1. Target Platform and Technology Stack Constraints
- Target platform: Linux x64 (Ubuntu / OSWorld Ubuntu VM).

- Technology stack: uniformly adopt `.NET 8 LTS self-contained + Avalonia UI 11 + MVVM/Command Pattern + SQLite local data storage + local mock service + app_data portable data directory + standard evaluation CLI`.
- Execution: the software package must be launchable locally via `release/run.sh` or an equivalent startup script.

- Data policy: user data, configuration, logs, mock data, and temporary exports are written by default to an `app_data/` directory inside or next to the software package, avoiding reliance on system-level installation paths.
## 2. Product Goals and MVP Boundaries

Clearly describe the core purpose of this software, target users, the foundational capabilities it must have compared to mainstream similar products, the local data policy, the core workflows that must be implemented, and the explicitly out-of-scope items. If a Software Positioning and Usage Description or Resource Directory Positioning Description was provided, explain in this section how it influences target users, core scenarios, and MVP boundaries. This section must read like a mature commercial product requirements document, not a development-test description or engineering constraint list.
## 3. Functional Requirements
Output by numbered modules using a format similar to the example below. The number of modules depends on the software type, but there must be at least six major modules.
### 3.1 Module Name
| Feature | User Action | Expected Underlying Result | Expected UI Result | Checkpoints |

| Feature name | Specific user operations | What the application should create, persist, update, or restore internally | What page, content, state, or prompt the user should see in the GUI | Prioritize GUI-observable acceptance; supplement with file or local data checks when necessary |
The following is an example style; actual content must be redesigned based on `{{software_type}}`—do not copy the example verbatim:
### 3.1 Launch and Local Identity
| Feature | User Action | Expected Underlying Result | Expected UI Result | Checkpoints |

| First launch of the application | Run `release/run.sh` and wait for the main window to open | Create the portable data directory, default configuration, and local demo data | The main window appears normally; if no local identity exists yet, show a getting-started or create-identity entry point; no external login blocking the flow | The GUI can enter the local identity creation flow; the window does not crash; supplement by checking the data directory exists when necessary |

| Create local identity | Enter a local username or work identity and click confirm | Save the current identity, initialize default demo data, and record the recent identity | Enter the main functional area; the entered nickname appears in the header, sidebar, or profile card; the default list or workspace is visible | An empty nickname cannot be submitted in the UI or shows an error; the GUI can restore the nickname after restart; supplement by checking local configuration when necessary |

| Switch or sign out of identity | Click switch / sign out in the settings or identity menu | Save current drafts and recent state, switch the current identity pointer | The UI returns to the identity selection / start page, or switches to the main interface of another identity; lists and histories of different identities are not mixed | The current identity name, contact/object list, and recent records in the GUI change with identity switching; local business data is not lost |
Finally, write only to: {{requirement_output_path}}
